Chichén Itzá. A major ceremonial center in the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico, representing the remarkable blending of Maya and Toltec cultures that flourished from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries. Located in Quintana Roo state in the northern Yucatan Peninsula, it was occupied from around 600 CE onward, but reached its greatest prominence during the Terminal Classic and Early Postclassic periods.

The site's most famous structure is El Castillo, the Castle—a seventy-nine-foot stepped pyramid dedicated to Kukulkan, the feathered serpent deity. The pyramid's architecture creates a stunning visual effect: during the spring and autumn equinoxes, shadows cast by the temple form the illusion of a serpent descending the pyramid's side.

The Great Ball Court here is the largest known Mesoamerican ball court, stretching five hundred forty-five feet long, where ritual ball games played a crucial role in religious and political ceremonies. Archaeological evidence suggests that losers of these games may have been ritually sacrificed. The site also contains the Cenote of Sacrifice, a natural sinkhole where excavations have revealed that both humans and precious objects were ritually thrown as offerings to Chaac, the rain god.

Chichén Itzá shows unmistakable evidence of Toltec influence alongside Maya design—columns carved as feathered serpents, warrior imagery, and architectural styles that differ distinctly from earlier Classic Maya sites. Throughout the site, Maya glyphs and astronomical alignments demonstrate sophisticated calendrical knowledge and mathematical precision, including both the three hundred sixty-five-day solar year and the two hundred sixty-day ritual calendar.

Today it stands as one of Mexico's most visited archaeological sites and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, drawing millions of tourists annually and exemplifying the cultural synthesis and astronomical sophistication of late Mesoamerican civilization.
